text:
The bookbinder lays a square of blue cloth on the table. With the flat of her hand she smooths it once, from the middle outward. A loose thread curls beside her thumb.

Sun reaches the jars of brushes. Their wooden handles have grown pale where hands have held them, and dark at the tips.

She sets the covered book beneath a board to dry. Then she turns her chair toward the open door. Across the courtyard, someone is shelling peas into a bowl. A few fall at a time: a small, round sound, with room around it.

Under the pear tree,
the grass is cool enough
to keep the shape of shade.

A chair stands with one foot
on a flat stone.
The wicker gives a little
when someone sits.

Above the chair, a pear
has ripened on one side.
Its yellow is the yellow
of butter left on a plate.

A bee works through the clover,
flower, then flower.
The tree moves its leaves
without moving its shade far.

On the chair's broad arm,
a hand lies open.
A small leaf lands there
and stays.

“Is that the blue you meant?”

“A little more grey, I think.”

He adds a touch to the glaze and draws the brush along a broken tile. They set it beside the bowl. Beyond the workshop window, pigeons walk the warm roof, lifting their feet as though the tiles were soft.

“That one,” she says.

The bowl turns slowly in his hands. The colour settles into the shallow ring beneath its rim.

Later, over bread and sliced tomatoes, she puts the sample tile between them. In the afternoon light it is the colour of the roof after rain.

A note from the island:

The small ferry still comes in stern first. This morning it brought two baskets of bread and a man with a young plum tree between his knees. He held the branches together while the baker carried the baskets ashore.

We had the round loaf on the step. The crust left flour on our fingers. Down at the landing, the ferryman rinsed his cup, and a silver line of water fell from it into the harbour.

The plum tree is beside the gate now. Its leaves make a patch of moving shade on the white wall.

By the time the sun reaches the kitchen floor, the rice is steaming. A boy carries the pot to the table with a folded cloth under each hand. His grandfather moves the cups aside.

They eat with the door open to the garden. A hen scratches beneath the beans. Now and then a leaf touches the doorframe.

After lunch the boy washes the pot. His grandfather dries it, turning it to find the water caught around the handles. He sets it upside down on its shelf.

The afternoon light reaches farther into the kitchen, across the clean table, as far as the empty cloths.
